ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
Schemes of National Horticulture Board 
*281. SHRI MATILAL SARKAR: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE 
be pleased to state: 
(a) the percentage of horticultural land in the country, State-wise; 
(b) the number of schemes implemented by the National Horticulture Board 
in the country and in the North-Eastem States; 
(c) the percentage of the horticultural produce processed during the years 
2002-03, 2003-04 and 2004-05; and 
(d) whether Government are planning for processing horticultural 
produce in a larger quantity to avoid wastage of the produce? 
THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI SHARAD PAWAR): (a) to 
(d) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) to (d) The State-wise percentage of area under horticultural crops with 
reference to total area under cultivation in the country is given in the 
Statement-I (See below). The National Horticulture Board is implementing 
five schemes in the country including North-Eastem States. These schemes are (i) 
Development of Commercial Horticulture through Production and Post-
harvest Management, (ii) Capital Investment Subsidy for 
Construction/Modernization/Expansion of Cold Storage and Storages for 
Horticulture Produce, (iii) Technol ogy Development and Transfer for 
Promotion of Horticulture, (iv) Market Information Service for 

RAJYA SABHA [12 August, 2005] 
Horticulture Crops and (v) Horticulture Promotion Services. The total 
quantity of fruit and vegetables processed during 2002-03, 2003-04 and 2004-
05 is 18 lakh tonnes, 20 lakh tonnes and 22 lakh tonnes respectively which is 
around 1:4 per cent of the production. The Ministry of Food Processing 
Industries is implementing Plan Schemes for encouraging development of 
food processing industries. The schemes includes (a) Technology 
Upgradation/Establishment/Modernization of Food Processing for which 
assistance is given in the form of grant, subject to 25% of the plant and 
machinery and technical civil works subject to a maximum of Rs. 50 lakhs in 
general areas and 33.33% upto Rs. 75 lakhs in difficult areas, and (b) Scheme 
for Infrastructure Development for Food Park for which assistance is given in 
the form of grant subject 25% of the project cost in general areas and 33.33% 
in difficult areas subject to a maximum of Rs. 4 crores for provision of 
common facilities like cold storage, food testing and analysis laboratory, 
effluent treatment plant, common processing facilities, power, water supply, 
etc.

SHRI MATILAL SARKAR: Sir, my first supplementary is, the total 
processed horticultural produce is stated to be 1.4 per cent only of the total 
agro-produce. But, Sir, in the Annual Report, the percentage appears to be fairly 
larger than what is stated here. Sir, particularly, in the North-East Region where 
there is heavy rainfall, if water catchment programme is taken extensively, more 
areas can be brought, under horticulture. Sir, my question is, why is the 
percentage comparatively so small in respect of horticulture? And, what steps 
the Government propose to take to expand the areas under horticulture, 
whatever it is possible? Because in Madhya Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh, Punjab, 
the percentage is very low. ...(Interruptions)... 
MR. CHAIRMAN: You have put your question. Let him reply. 
...(Interruptions)... 
SHRI MATILAL SARKAR: This seems to be very low. What is the 
programme of the Government in this regard? 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Mr. Sarkar, you have put the question. Let him reply. 
SHRI SHARAD PAWAR: Mr. Chairman, Sir, the production figure of 1.4 
per cent which the hon. Member has given is not the country's production. 
This figure of 1.4 per cent is in respect of processed production. Out of total 
production, only 1.4 per cent is processed. That is why we are very weak in 
agro-processing area. That is the reas on, we have introduced a number of 
schemes through agro-processing units. 
The second thing which the hon. Member has asked is how to increase the area 
under horticulture. In fact, this is the reason why the new scheme has been 
introduced, i.e., the Horticulture Mission, where a substantial monetary 
provision has been made, and in five year time, we would like to double the 
total area under horticulture in the country. 
SHRI MATILAL SARKAR: Sir, my s econd supplementary is this. The 
setting up of processing units for fruits and vegetables may be encouraged 
among the youth through self-employment schemes. These youth should be 
specially trained for this purpose; and they should be extended financial 
facilities through banks. What is the programme in 
4 

[12 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
this regard? Is there any programme wi th the Government to encourage the 
youth for self-employment in the field of food processing? 
SHRI SHARAD PAWAR: Sir, the programme under the Ministry of Food 
Processing is like this. In fact, as I said, the total capacity of the fruit and 
vegetable processing industry on the 1 st of January, 2005 is 19.24 lakh 
tonnes only. What the Government has decided is to encourage this sector. 
That is why a number of decisions have been taken. For instance, recently, in 
order to give boost to the growth of food processing industry, the Government 
has allowed under the Income-Tax Act, a deduction of hundred per cent of 
profit for five years and twenty-five per cent profit for the next five years. 
That is one of the decisions which the Government has taken just to 
encourage various sections. In addition to it, there are some other schemes, 
where some subsidy has been provided to those who are going to set up a 
specific unit which will be useful for ag ro-processing or fruit-processing or 
vegetable-processing. There is no specific scheme for younger generation. 
These schemes are available for everybody.

ANBUMANI RAMDOSS): (a) to (c) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
According to Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR), Sickle Cell disease is 
prevalent in various States in different parts of the country including Chhattisgarh. 
Though a number of deaths occur in Chhattisgarh due to this disease, the ICMR and the 
Government of Chhattisgarh have informed that there is no authentic data available in 
this regard. The disease is a genetic disorder due to defective haemoglobin structure and is 
generally prevalent in the tribal areas. This being a hereditary disease, prevention is the 
only remedy available which includes creating awareness in the affected region. 
The Chhattisgarh Government has informed that a decision has already been taken by the 
State Government to establish Sickle Cell Solubility Test Facilities at all the sector, 
block and district level Government hospitals along with Haemoglobin 
Electrophoresis facilities at all the district level Government hospitals for detection of 
Sickle Cell disorders. In addition, ICMR has informed that testing facilities have been 
set up at Raipur Medical College under ICMR WHO programme to screen antenatal 
pregnant women for prevalence of Sickle Cell anaemia.

project reports are to be submitted by the State Government as per the Master 
Plan, the preparation of which has been entrusted to a professional agency by 
the State Government.

(a) to (d) 71 river stretches are polluted inter-alia due to discharge of domestic and

industrial and other sources include notifying industry specific effluent standards, 
promoting setting up of common effluent treatment plants and environmental 
surveillance by the Central Pollution Control Board, State Pollution Control Boards 
and Pollution Control Committees, besides improving the quality of water in major 
rivers through the National River Conservation Plan (NRCP). Under the NRCP, pollution 
abatement works are undertaken including diversion and interception of sewage, 
installation of sewerage treatment plants, etc. A seweage treatment capacity of 865

been created and subsequent to that, another 1421 mid capacity will the end of the

river Yamuna, the water quality has shown improvement except for a few stretches. 
2. Monitoring of water quality in the Yamuna has shown that in the lean season 
(March-June) during the year 2004, the Biochemical Oxygen Demand (BOD) in the 
stretch of the river between Wazirabad and Okhla barrage in Delhi has been as high

aquatic life. This is partly due to lack of fresh water in the river downstream of 
Wazirabad barrage. River conservation programme in the form of Yamuna Action 
Plan-I as part of the NRCP was also initially taken up on the river Yamuna which is

Development have also prepared an Integrated Action Plan to be implemented by 
different agencies of the Central Government and the State Government of the NCT 
of Delhi, which includes components under YAP-II.

Target for agricultural growth 
*285. SHRI SANJAY RAUT: Will th e Minister of AGRICULTURE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have set a targ et to increase th e annual growth 
rate of agricultural production by more than 6.5 per cent for coming years; 
(b) if so, the details of measures taken or proposed to be taken for 
increasing growth of agricultural products in the country; and 
(c) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI SHARAD PAWAR): (a) to (c) 
A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) No, Sir. In its Mid-Term appraisal of .the Tenth Five Year Plan (2002-
2007), the Planning Commission has projected growth of GDP at 2001-02 
prices in agriculture, including allied sectors of forestry and logging, and 
fishing, at 4.0 per cent and 3.2 per cent during 2005-06 and 2006-07 
respectively. 
(b) and (c) As indicated in the Mid-Term Appraisal of the Tenth Plan, the 
growth rate in 2002-03 the first year of the Tenth Plan was negative (-6.8 per 
cent) which reflected the impact of the severe drought that adversely affected 
agricultural production in several States/regions in the country. Favourable 
weather facilitated revival of agricultural growth, which improved to 9.5% in 
2003-04. However, in the subsequent year, i.e. 2004-05 serious deficiency in 
rainfall led to deterioration in performance in the agriculture sector, and as a 
result, growth rate in agriculture decelerated to 1.1 per cent. The inability of 
Indian agriculture to withstand weather related shocks mainly reflects the fact 
that there has been steady decline in public investment in real terms in 
agriculture, including allied sectors, over successive Five Year Plans. This in 
turn reflects decline in investment towards irrigation and water management. 
With a view to increase agricultural production, Government has adopted 
a multi progned strategy for addressing  specific segments of agriculture to 
ensure higher productivity. These initiatives are in the areas 
29 

RAJYA SABHA [12 August, 2005] 
of both cereal and non-cer eal crops, horticulture, livestock, fisheries and 
dairying. Equal emphasis is also been given to timely availability of inputs and 
an overall thrust towards diversification into higher value produces and 
plantations. Initiatives taken towards these areas include launch of the National 
Horticulture Mission, undertaking activities with a Mission approach for 
enhancing productivity and quality of cotton, oilseeds, pulses and coarse 
grains. The Union Budget for 2005-06 has underscored the importance of 
providing enhanced credit coverage to the farming community as a 
consequence of which Rs. 1,15,242 Crores was disbursed in 2004-05. Credit 
flow to agriculture will be stepped up by another 30% in 2005-06. Initiatives 
has also been taken to include micro irrigation, enhanced provisions for the 
accelerated irrigation technology progra mme, strengthening of agricultural 
marketing infrastructure, development of backward and forward linkages 
through venture capital support and facilitations to growers association for 
producing larger and better quality of fruits, flowers and vegetables. 
Determined efforts are also being made to increase fisheries production largely 
through inland aquaculture. Livestock and Dairying have also received 
greater attention through enhanced budget outlays as well as defined policies 
towards cross-breeding and delineation of disease free zones.

in the country; if so, the details thereof and if not, the reasons therefor; 
(d) whether it is a fact that the Prime Minister announced during the meeting that 
the Population Policy of the country does not encourage incentives and 
disincentives; and 
(e) if so, the manner in which Government propose to control 
population without any incentives and disincentives? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. 
ANBUMANI RAMADOSS): (a) to (c) Yes, Sir. The first meeting of the reconstituted 
National Commission on Population (NCP) was held under the Chairmanship of the 
Hon'ble Prime Minister on 23rd July, 2005. The meeting discussed the following 
items: 
0) Approach to issues of Population Stabilisation based on National 
Common Minimum Programme (NCMP); 
(ii) Learning from Southern States; and 
(iii) Population challenge in demographically weaker States and appropriate 
Strategies. 
In course of detailed discussions on the agenda items, the importance of providing need 
based, client centered, demand driven and high quality services to the beneficiaries, while 
recognizing the need for empowerment of women and their right to make informed 
choices, was emphasized. Such services would enhance the quality of reproductive 
life of the population enabling country to achieve the goal of population stabilization. The 
following two decisions were taken: 
(i) There should be an Annual Health Survey of all districts, which could be 
published annually so that health indicators at district level are periodically 
published, monitored and compared against benchmarks. 
(ii) The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare should set up five groups of 
experts for studyingxthe population profile of the States of Bihar, Uttar 
Pradesh, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh and Orissa to identify weaknesses 
in the health delivery

systems and to suggest measures that would be taken to improve the 
health and demographic status of the States. 
(d) and (e) Yes, Sir. The tenet of the Population Policy regarding voluntary and 
informed choice while availing of family welfare services, without any 
incentive/disincentive was emphasized at the meeting. 
Providing incentives and disincentives are not very relevant for population 
stabilization measures. As a matter of fact, on occasions, they can prove to be counter 
productive. The population stabilization requires a holistic approach to the problem. The 
Government has recently launched National Rural Health Mission (NRHM), which seeks to 
provide integrated comprehensive primary healthcare services, especially to the poor and 
vulnerable sections of the society throughout the country with special focus on 18 
States. The objective of the NRHM is to provide accessible and reliable primary 
health care services so as to achieve the Goals of National Population Policy and

†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi.

Prevention of Food Adulteration (PFA) Rules, 1955, the names of ingredients used 
in the product shall be declared on the label in descending order of their composition 
by weight or volume as the case may be. Similar provisions have been prescribed by Codex 
Alimeniarious Commission which is an international organization for standardization of 
food products. All the countries in the world follow the practice of declaration of 
the ingredients on the label. 
Pesticides are not used as an ingredient in preparation of any food products. 
Pesticide residues comes in food through use of pesticides upon food crops or during 
storage of food grains. As stated above, there is no practice in any country or any 
provisions under CODEX to display the extent of pesticides on the label of food items. 
There is. therefore, no proposal under consideration for displaying limit of pesticides on 
the label of food items under PFA Rules, 1955. 
In order that the contaminants in food products do not exceed the safe limits, the 
maximum tolerance limits for pesticide residues in food products have been prescribed 
under prevention of Food Adulteration (PFA) Rules, 1955, Any violation of the limits 
prescribed is punishable under law. 
Studies have been conducted by Ministry of Health and Family Welfare during the 
years 1988-89,1993-94 and 2000-01. All these studies reveal that the pesticide residues 
detected in various foods are within the tolerance limits prescribed under the PFA 
Rules, 1955, except in some cases where the residues exceeded the prescribed limits.

forecast), 2.8 per cent (low forecast), and 3.2 per cent (high forecast) in 2005-

The thrust of agriculture policy continues to be on schemes and 
programmes designed to raise production and productivity in agriculture 
through transfer of improved technology based on field demonstrations, 
training of farmers, supply of qua lity inputs, improvement in irrigation 
facilities, pest control measures etc. The centrally sponsored scheme, namely, 
Macro Management, was evolved by integrating 27 schemes. Under this 
scheme, which is designed to supplement/complement efforts put in by States, 
there is flexibility to develop and pursue activities through Work Plans based

in the ratio of 90:10 for the Centre a nd States except in the case of North-

for contraception, health care infrastructure, and health personnel and to provide 
integrated service delivery for basic reproductive and child health care. The 
medium-term objective is to bring the Total Fertility Rate (TFR) to

preferably after 20 years of age. 
* Achieve universal access to inform ation/counselling, and services 
for fertility regulation and contr aception with a wide basket of 
choices.

of TFR.

doubling the flow of credit in three years, enhancing the coverage of 
institutional credit through Kisan Credit Cards, restructuring of loans etc.

Price Hike of Diabetes and Tuberculosis Drugs 
2070. SHRI VAYALAR RAVI: Will th e Minister of CHEMICALS AND 
FERTILIZERS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that the prices of certain life saving drugs 
and the drugs for diabetes and tuberculosis have increased after introducing 
the patent regim; and 
(b) if so, what steps have been taken to check this abnormal increase of drug 
prices? 
THE MINISTER OF CHEMICALS AND FERTILIZERS (SHRI RAM 
VILAS PASWAN): (a) and (b) The Drugs (Prices Control) Order, 1995 
(DPCO, 95) does not make any distinction between Life Saving drugs and 
other drugs. There is no specific norms or guidelines to determine as to which 
drugs can be classified as life saving drugs. Every drug , in general, is 
considered useful in saving and prolonging of life. 
The 74 bulk drugs specified in the First Schedle of the Drugs (Prices 
Control) Order, 1995 (DPCO, 95) and the formulations based thereon are 
under price control and their prices are fixed/revised by the National 
Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA)  in accordance with the provisions 
of the DPCO,95. These drugs have been identified for inclusion under price 
control in the DPCO, 95 on the basis of criteria mentioned in the 'Modification 
in Drug Policy, 1986', announced in September, 1994. These criteria take into 
account the extent of usage and the market competition of various drugs. 
Prices of non-Scheduled formulations are fixed by the manufacturers 
themselves keeping in view the various factors like cost of production, 
marketing/selling expenses, R&D expenses, trade commission, market 
competition, product innovation, product quality etc. The Government takes 
corrective measures where the public interest is found to be adversely 
affected. 
Under DPCO, 1995 the bulk drugs Glipizide and Insulin which are used 
for treatment of Diabetes, and bulk drugs Rifampicin and Streptomycin 
which are used for treatment of Tuberculosis are under price control. So far 
as the prices of these Scheduled bulk  drugs and formulations based thereon 
are concerned, there has not been any increase after introduction of the patent 
regime w.e.f. 1-1-2005.

2073. SHRIMATI JAYA BACHCHAN: Will the Minister of CHEMICALS

criteria take into account the extent of usage and the market competition in 
various drugs. 
Prices of non-Scheduled formulations are fixed by the manufacturers 
themselves keeping in view the various factors like cost of production, 
marketing/selling expenses, R&D expe nses, trade commission, market 
competition, product innovation, product quality etc. Due to these factors there is 
a wide variation between the production cost and selling price of these 
medicines. The Government takes co rrective measures where the public 
interest is found to be adversely affected.

Steps taken by Government for protection and conservation of tigers 
and other wildlife 
Steps taken by the Government for protection and conservation of tigers 
and other wildlife are as under: 
(i) Legal protection has been provided to wild animals against hunting and 
commercial exploitation under the provisions of the Wildlife 
(Protection) Act, 1972. 
(ii) Several rare and endangered sp ecies of wild animals have been 
included in the Schedules of Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, 
thereby giving it highest degree of protection. 
(iii) The Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 has been amended and made more 
stringent. The punishment in cases of offences has been enhanced. 
The Act also provides for forfeiture of any equipment, vehicle or 
weapon that has been used for committing any wildlife offence. 
122 

[12 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(iv) Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) has been empowered under the 
Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 to apprehended and prosecute wildlife 
offenders.

wildlife preservation in major export and trade centres of the country 
to prevent smuggling of wild animals and their products. 
(vi) Financial and technical help is provided to the States under various 
Centrally Sponsored Schemes, viz. Project Tiger, Project Elephant and 
Development of National Parks and Sanctuaries for enhancing the capacity 
and infrastructure of the States for providing effective protection to wild 
animals. 
(vii) A National Wildlife Action Plan, 2002—16 was adopted by the 
Indian Board for Wildlife under the Chairmanship of Prime Minister in 
January, 2002. The plan outlines the strategy for conservation and 
protection of wildlife in the country. 
(viii) Government of India is a signatory to many international 
conventions concerning biodiversity conservation and control of 
illegal trade in wild flora and fauna. 
(ix) Bilateral agreements have been signed with Nepal and Republic of 
China for controlling trans-boundary illegal trade in wildlife. 
(x) A Global Tiger Forum of tiger ra nge countries has been created for 
addressing international issues related to tiger conservation. 
(xi) A proposal for creating a Wildlife Crime Control Bureau has been made.

Statement-IV 
Steps taken for Protection of Tigers and other wildlife The following 
measures have been taken at the Govemment of India level to protect tiger and 
other wild animals: 
(i) Legal protection has been provided to wild animals including tigers 
against hunting and commercial exploitation under the provisions 
of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972. (ii) Financial and technical help 
is being extended to the States under 
Centrally Sponsored Schemes for enhancing the capacity and 
infrastructure to provide effective protection to wild animals, (iii) The 
Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) has been empowered 
under the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 to apprehend and 
prosecute wildlife offenders, (iv) The Ministry of Home Affairs has 
addressed all State Governments 
to lend a helping hand to the field formations to curb poaching 
and illegal trade in wildlife. 
137 

RAJYA SABHA [12 August, 2005] 
(v) A National Wildlife Action Plan (2002-2016) has been launched with 
several action points and priority projects for conservation and protection of 
wildlife in the country. 
(vi) Independent monitoring of tiger reserves has been done by a panel of 
experts drawn as per the normative guidelines of the Ministry. A 
standardized format for evaluation has been prescribed for monitoring and 
evaluation, based on the framework of the World Commission of Protected 
Areas (IUCN). 
(vii) A tiger habitat and population evaluation system' has been developed in the 
GIS domain, with inputs from the scientists of Wll, involving the state 
officials and field staff. Based on this, the Project Tiger Directorate of the 
Ministry has refined the procedure with a peer review mechanism comprising of 
independent experts, both national and international (IUCN) for overseeing the 
primary data collection. 
(viii) Tiger presence and its breeding status have been mapped for the entire 
country at taluk level amplification in the GIS domain for an assessment 
of habitat fragmentation.

Dengue and Japanese Encephalitis at this juncture.

to eliminate Lymphatic Filariasis by the year 2015. To pursue this goal, Govt, has 
decided to administer single dose of Dtethylcarbmagine (DEC) tablet (anti filarial drug) 
to the entire population in the filaria endemic districts except children below 2- years, 
pregnant women and sick persons continuosly for a minimum period of 5 years 
through a campaign of Mass Drug Administration. During 2004, Mass Drug 
Administration with DEC was implemented in 202 filaria endemic districts covering a 
population of about 407 million in 20 States/UTs. During 2005, all 259 endemic 
districts will observe National Filaria Day on 11 th November followed by mopping up 
operations on 12-13 November for improving the drug compliance by the community. 
Morbidity management of lymphoedema cases is implemented through foot hygiene by 
simple methods to be observed by the patients. Hydrocele operations are

Problem of leprosy in India 
2127. SHRI RAVI SHANKAR PRASAD: Will the Minster of HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that India has the highest burden of leprosy in the world; 
(b) if so, what is the extent of this menace indicating the sensitive regions in the 
country; and 
(c) what is the action plan of Government to control this desease? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) The total number of recorded cases in India at the end of March, 2005 were 
1,48,910 and the Prevalence Rate of Leprosy at the end of March, 2005 was 1.34 
per 10,000 population. In 11 States/UTs Prevalence Rate of leprosy is between 1-
4/10,000 population. These States/UTs are Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Chandigarh, D 
& N Haveli and Delhi, Bihar, Goa, Maharashtra, Orissa, U.R and West Bengal. In 
rest of the 24 States/UTs the level of elimination i.e. Prevalence Rate of less than 1 
per 10,000 population has been achieved. 
(c) The Government of India is implementing the National Leprosy Eradication 
Programme for the elimination of leprosy from the country. The details of the 
scheme are:— 
(i) Decentralization and Institutional Development under which State 
Leprosy Societies have been formed in 27 major States and District 
Leprosy Societies in all the Districts in the country which are responsible 
for proper planning, implementation, monitoring and timely 
corrective action. 
160 

[12 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(ii) Integration of Leprosy Services  with General Health Care System 
in the country for better out-reach and utilization of services by 
community. 
(Hi) Early Leprosy Case Detection and Free Multi Drug Therapy to all 
patients through all Government Primary Health Centres, 
Dispensaries and Hospitals in the country. 
Civ) Intensified Public Awareness Campaigns through Mass Media as 
well as local media at periphery. 
(v) Training of General Health Care Staff in leprosy and in disability 
prevention and Care. 
(vi) Prevention of Deformities and Care. 
Government has set a target of achieving leprosy elimination level i.e. 
Prevalence Rate of less than 1 case per 10,000 population at the national 
level by the end of 2005.

for fulfilling the objective of National Common Minimum Programme to ensure the

intensive monitoring on the prices of all those drugs out of the selected basket (National

margins of drugs a system of price negotiations for the new patented drugs, special 
schemes for people below poverty line, introduction of Rajasthan Model of Life Line

2. For achieving these goals, the Reproductive and Child Health

since 1997. A number of interventions are being implemented for improving 
the maternal and child health and bringing down mortality rates as part of this 
programme. 
3. The interventions for improving maternal health are (i) essential 
obstetric care, (ii) emer gency obstetric care, (iii) referral transport for

equipments at First Referral Units (FRUs), (v) Provision of contractual staff like 
addition Auxiliary Nurse Midwife (ANMs), (vi) staff nurses and hiring of 
anaesthetists, In the second phase of the RCH Programme, provision has been 
made to accelerate the decline of Maternal Mortality and Morbidity by 
introducing new interventions like operationaiisation of First Referral Units 
(FRUs), providing 24-hour delivery and new born care services at Community 
Health Centres (CHCs) and Primary Health Centres (PHCs) and training of 
ANM and LHV to become skill birth attendants.

Vitamin A deficiency and (vi) essential new born care. As part of the second 
phase of RCH Programme, the Integrated Management for Newborn and 
Childhood Illness (IMNCI) will be implemented in the districts in phased 
manner.

Mission (NRHM) in order to improve the availability of land access to quality 
health care including services for Immunization and Safe Motherhood. The 
mission seeks to provide effective health care to rural population throughout the

Assam, Bihar, Chhattisgarh, Himachal Pradesh, Jharkhand, Jammu & Kashmir,

every village with a population up to  1000. ASHA will facilitate in 
accessing hearth care services to  the community and will have 
specific responsibility of mobilizing pregnant women for ante-natal 
care institutional delivery and post-natal checks and immunization to

Units (FRU) for providing Emergency Obstetric and Child Health 
services.

2166. SHRI VEDPRAKASH P. GOYAL: Will the Minister of RAILWAYS 
be pleased to state: 
(a) the procedure of discharging inquiry reports submitted by the Commission of 
Railway Safety; 
(b) how many inquiry reports have been submitted by the Commission during the last

and

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS (SHRI R. VELU): 
(a) Commissioners of Railway Safety submit two reports of each enquiry into railway 
accidents. Preliminary Report indicates provisional findings and immediate 
recommendations. Final Report, containing cause of the accident, responsibility 
therefor and recommendations is submitted to Chief Commissioner of Railway Safety 
and copies thereof are forwarded to Railway Board and railway administration of 
zonal Railways and other Commissioners of Railway Safety. Railway administration of 
the concerned Railway initiates action on the report and submits his comments to the 
Chief Commissioner of Railway Safety. Chief Commissioner of Railway Safety submits 
remarks on the Final Report to the Ministry of Railways after scrutinizing the 
comments of concerned railway administration. Ministry of Railways takes a final view 
on the report and comments of the Chief Commissioner of Railway Safety thereon and 
directs zonal railways administrations to implement accepted recommendations. 
(b) and (c) During the last one year from 1.4.04 to 31.3.05, total 19 inquiry reports 
have been submitted by the Commission. As per these inquiry reports, 10 accidents 
were caused due to failure of Railway

staff, 6 were caused due to the failure of other then Railway staff and 3 
accidents were due to equipment failure and incidental. 
(d) Safety is the prime -concern of Indian Railways and adoption of new 
measures to improve safety Is a continuous process. Measures being taken by 
Indian Railways to minimize incide nce of accidents include adoption of 
suitable modern technology for interlocking and signaling system, 
upgradation of standards of track and rolling stock, modernization of

Demand to Recognise Services of Those who Rescue Persons 
in Distress 
SHRI S.S. AHLUWALIA (Jharkhand): Sir, human history is full of instances where 
driven by passion and sympathy, man has rescued his fellow men from distress and peril 
and, I think, any such kind acts of man anywhere on this earth should be 
highlighted not only to acknowledge such good acts but also to provoke others to 
imbibe it. 
Sir, on 10th July, 2005, a marriage party comprising ninety Christian priests travelling 
in a truck met with an accident on its way from Jamankeri village to Goudpil in 
Sambalpur district in Orissa, in which 10 persons died instantly and the remaining 80 
survivors, who were still struggling for life, trapped in the ill-fated truck in a dense forest, 
were rescued by some dedicated social workers who responded to the emergency 
after hearing their cry for help. 
Importantly, credit for this noble humanitarian act that saved eighty precious lives 
goes to a group of volunteers of the local Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh, i.e. R.S.S., 
who rushed to the accident spot and rescued the survivors from the trap without 
considering their caste, creed or religion. 
Sir, this incident brings forth the memory of the incident of crash of a plane carrying 
Haj pilgrims near Charkhi Dadri village, some years back. Soon after take-off from Delhi 
Airport, the plane had crashed. The first rescuers of the survivors were the volunteers of 
the local R.S.S. who were holding their 'shakhas' there. 
I urge upon the Government to appreciate and highlight such noble acts whenever 
and wherever committed by mankind. Thank you, Sir.

Demand for granting exemption from excise duty on industrial units being set up 
in tsunami-affected districts of Tamil Nadu 
SHRIMATI S.G INDIRA (Tamil Nadu): The State Government of Tamil Nadu had done 
everything possible to rehabilitate the tsunami-affected people in the State of Tamil Nadu. 
Tamil Nadu was the most affected State in the recent tsunami. Many measures had 
been taken by the Government of Tamil Nadu to accelerate reconstruction in the tsunami-
hit Tiruvallur, Kancheepuram, Cuddalore, Nagapattinam, Tuticorin and Kanyakumari 
districts. However, it is the process of reconstruction of infrastructure and revitalisation of 
the economy of these districts which alone can ultimately bring real normalcy back to 
these areas. Many international organisations were providing assistance in this 
process. However, there is a need to give a big push to revitalising this economy of the 
tsunami-affected districts as demanded by the hon. Chief Minister of Tamil Nadu. The 
Government of Tamil Nadu had sought to issue a notification granting exemption from 
excise levies for ten years from the date of commercial production on all excisable goods 
manufactured by the industrial units established in the tsunami-affected districts within 
three years from the date of notification. Such exemption had been granted in the past in 
Kutch, Gujarat, Himachal Pradesh and Uttaranchal. The exemption would attract large-
scale investment from corporate industrial houses to restore and improve 
infrastructure and establish industrial units in the tsunami-hit districts. 
Therefore, I urge upon the Government to grant ten years' exemption from excise levies 
as demanded by the hon. Chief Minister for the units to be established in the tsunami-
affected districts in Tamil Nadu. 
SHRI S.P.M. SYED KHAN (Tamil Nadu): Sir, I associate myself with the hon. 
Member. 
SHRI R. KAMARAJ (Tamil Nadu): Sir, I too associate myself with the hon. Member.

Demand for continuation of the CGHS for the Retired and serving government 
employees in the country 
SHRI A. VIJAYARAGHAVAN (Kerala): Sir, the Central Government Health Scheme 
(CGHS) is on the verge of closure. More than 45-lakh servicing employees, 5-lakh 
pensioners, former Governors, freedom fighters, Ministers, Judges and Members of 
Parliament are the beneficiaries of the CGHS. It is serving in 24 cities. Sir, the CGHS 
is having 246 dispensaries, 19 polyclinics, 18 laboratories and 86 ISM units in the 
country. The annual Budget of the CGHS is Rs.600 crores. 
It is reported in the newspapers that the CGHS would be replaced with "Health Card" 
through insurance companies. Whereas, the insurance sector has already been privatised. 
The Government has allowed 84 per cent FDI in insurance sector. Hence, the "Health 
Card" would be a hounding ground for corporate and multinational insurance companies.

comprehensive healthcare for its employees.

Need to take steps to make India a 
Pollution free country 
SHRIMATI SYEDAANWARA TAIMUR (Assam): Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, 
pollution has become a major problem in our country. Serious pollutants 
including chemical plants, oil refineries, nuclear waste dumps, regular garbage 
dumps, incinerators, PVC, car factories, plastic factories etc. are creating huge 
amounts of pollution. The nitrogen oxides produced by the industry are often 
referred to as pollution, although the substances themselves are not harmful. In 
fact, it is the solar energy (sunlight) that converts these compounds into smog. 
Recycling of garbage and other waste has become necessary because 
landfills are closed and it is causing increasing damage to the environment. 
Without recycling of garbage, landfills can cause serious air and water 
pollution. 
Landfills can pollute lakes and other wate r bodies that may affect fisheries 
in addition to spreading water borne diseases. Decomposition of waste in 
landfills releases methane which can kill vegetation. 
So, I would like to request the Govern ment to enact such a law and give 
strict directions to the States to introduce garbage clearance by automatic 
system and to take initiative to plan for garbage or town waste re-cycling 
system and make many useful by-products from waste. This will create many 
job opportunities for the unemployed youth, the economy of the country will 
also develop, and India can become a pollution free country. It will prevent 
spreading of many epidemics or di seases and improve the health of the 
people of this country.

SHRI V. NARAYANASAMY (Pondicherry): The National Sample Survey 
Organisation conducted survey of about 51,000 farm households throughout the country to 
find out whether they would like to continue in agriculture or migrate to the urban areas 
for employment. 
There is an alarming situation prevailing in the rural area that about 40 per 
cent of the farmers wanted to quit agriculture and migrate to urban areas for living. The 
survey was conducted at the behest of the Agriculture Ministry from January to December,

villages. Nearly 60 per cent of the households liked farming as a profession,

farmers did not know that they have to insure their crops. The report further indicates 
that only 16 per cent farmers are aware of bio-fertilisers. Irrigated area is 42 per cent 
during Kharif season and 56 per cent during Rabi season. Tube wells are used as a major 
irrigation facility. 
The farmers would like to quit farming because the younger generation did

expedite creation of rural infrastructure by giving priority so that large-scale migration of 
the people from farming community to the urban areas could be contained.

Demand for central directive to all the state governments for 
fair and proper functioning of the state public service 
commissions in their states. 
SHRI TARLOCHAN SINGH (Haryana): Sir, with your permission, I am making this 
Special Mention regarding Public Service Commissions. Sir, Indian Constitution under 
Article 315 has prescribed that there will be a Public Service Commission both at the 
Centre and as well as in the States for recruitment to the civil services and civil posts. 
The members are appointed by the Government both at the Centre and the State 
Governments through a prescribed procedure. 
It has appeared in the Press that certain State Governments are trying to deprive 
the commissions to play their desired role with the excuse that the Members of the 
Commissions were appointed by the previous Government and the present Government 
belonging to a different political party does not repose trust in them. If we carry on our 
political battles like this and cast aspersions on the integrity of the persons holding 
such high constitutional positions, it will create an irreparable damage to the working of 
the democratic system. In the end, we may reach a situation where we have to amend 
our Constitution so that all persons appointed by a Government have to leave their jobs 
with the change of the Government. 
It is high time that the Parliament considers this threat to our system. I would like to 
draw the attention of the Government to give respect to the Constitutional bodies by 
issuing a directive to the States to desist from such activities. Thank you.

THE IMMIGRATION (CARRIERS' LIABILITY) 
AMENDMENT BILL, 2005 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS (SHRI 
S. REGUPATHY): Sir, I move: 
That the Bill to amend the Immigration (Carriers' Liability) Act, 2000, be 
taken into consideration. 
Sir, the Act places on carriers' the lia bility in respect of foreigners brought 
by them in contravention of the Passport  (Entry into India) Act, 1920 and the 
Rules made thereunder. The necessary of the new legislation was felt 
because a large number of passengers at the major international airports were 
found to be coming without valid travel documents, creating problems for 
immigration authorities. It was observed that carriers, airlines, etc. did not 
exercise proper checks of travel documents before allowing passengers to board 
planes in places outside India. It was, therefore, considered necessary to place 
statutory responsibility on carriers, airl ines, etc. bringing passengers not in 
possession of valid travel documents by imposing financial liability on them to 
the tune of one lakh of rupees per passenger brought by them without any valid 
travel documents, for which five exemptions have been given in respect of those 
who come without any valid travel documents. 
One is where the passenger had arrived on a flight or a ship which, 
following departure, had been diverted to India for reasons beyond the control 
of the carriers. An6ther is where a fo reigner has been exempted from the 
requirement of passport or visa by the Central Government. The third one is 
where the passengers are stowaways and the carrier is ready to take its 
passengers back. The fourth one is where a group of foreign tourists, 
consisting of four or more persons sponsored by recognised Indian travel 
agencies, arrive without visa, being authorised on collective visa, that is, permit 
issued to the whole group. The fifth one is where foreigners hold diplomatic or 
official passport and are exempt from the requirements of the visa. For these 
reasons, this amendment has been brought forward.

SHRI JANARDHANA POOJARY (Karnataka): Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, I am standing 
today before the House after seeing the TV programme the other day. At the 
conclusion of the debate there, when the anchor put the question, then one boy 
stated, These Parliament Members are begging, give them." That was the statement 
made by one boy in the debate. Sir, after seeing that, I was subjected to mental 
agony. It was painful and it was intimidating also. So far as the salary was concerned, 
there never used to be any debate in the House. Sometimes, our friends from the Left 
Party used to make a statement that they opposed; we never used to discuss. Sir, 
before starting, I am just bringing to your notice what the Members of Parliament of 
Australia are getting. They are getting $90,000 per annum. If we calculate it at the 
rate of Rs. 45 per dollar, it will come to Rs. 40,50,000/- per annum — more than 
Rs. 3 lakh. So far as the United Kingdom is concerned, they are getting $85,983. In 
Canada, they are getting $68,200 per annum. If we take into consideration Rs. 45 
per dollar, it will run into lakhs. And, what are we getting here? We are getting only 
Rs. 12,000/-. I thank Mr. Suri, I do not know whether he is a self-made man. He 
has taken into consideration the plight of the spouse after the retirement or after the 
death. I don't know whether he has faced any difficulty in his younger age. But what is 
happening in other countries? If you take into consideration these figures, what are 
we getting? Only Rs. 12,000/-! When I entered after the sixth term, I got Rs. 
12,000/- salary after putting in 27 years of service in the Parliament. Is any officer 
getting this much? Even a chaprasi will be getting more than that, But we are not 
begging. We never ask anything for sevice to the. people. When I started my 
practice in 1960, I was getting this amount per day. I am not from a rich family. 
When I used to go to school, I had only trousers, no shirt even. There were no two 
meals. When I completed my law, there was no money for me. I used to take water 
from the public pipe. And you may not believe, Sir, I did not have the money, I came 
from a very poor family, I used to live on one plantain per day. I had nothing. I became 
a lawyer. I had a roaring practice. I had a car. I had everything. I remained the Minister 
of State in the Ministry of Finance for six years and one month. That is a record. I did 
not take a glass of water from any person. I did not make even a single pie. And, Mr. 
V.P Singh is on record stating, "I come from a rich family, but Poojary comes from a 
poor family". But I remained honest. It is not a big thing. Poojary
